lead: someone is introduced to you for ninety seconds at a party, and you leave with two complete readings of them, both exact, both permanent, and nothing anywhere in you for putting one of them second.
sun: first contact hands most people one impression, and a second look is what revises it. you take two at the meeting itself, and neither is provisional — one has him as somebody you would leave a child with, the other has the precise week he would fail to turn up, both assembled in the same ninety seconds off the same evidence, and both kept.
moon: a stranger from one evening in your thirties is still in you at the sharpness of that evening, and so is the second reading of him — the pair arrived together and neither has slackened. no later meeting ever came to settle which one was nearer. you met a man once and acquired two whole people, and he left carrying nothing of you.
pull: two entire versions of everybody you have met once, neither of them checkable, and the person himself walked out of that room holding nothing at all.
tension: the question after any introduction is what you made of her, and it wants one word. you have two, and offering both sounds like somebody hedging in advance. so the warm half gets handed over, which is true, and the other stays in place at its original sharpness for eleven years — and when she does exactly what it said she would, the people who asked will remember being told she was lovely.
cost: ninety seconds gives you a person's best and the shape of their worst, and twenty years on both still fit. the ordinary generous mistake is what nobody gets from you — the friend taken up on faith, wrong about, forgiven for it. everyone you have ever liked was liked while the account of how they will fail sat beside it, undimmed.

lead: two people made this place, in opposite directions, and could not sit in a room together. you were brought up by both of them, and the seat you now hold descends from one line only.
sun: neither line is a half of anything. the years spent restoring what the first of them wanted, you wanted entirely; the years spent dismantling it are the whole of you as well, and the two are two intact inheritances executed in turn by one occupant. a committee reading the minutes across a decade finds somebody who keeps changing sides, and no minute of it records a person in two minds.
moon: the carriage does not vary between them. each is announced in the same level voice, from the same posture, so nothing in the room registers a switch as it happens, and the building's habit of not questioning the seat means nobody has ever raised the sequence with you. it accumulates instead — a decade of it, filed, unasked, available whole on the afternoon somebody decides to ask.
pull: no one else ever received the whole place, both halves of it, and the seat speaks in one voice, so you have been handing it over in instalments that read as reversals.
tension: the building sorts everyone by which of the two trained them, and both sides read you as one of theirs, on evidence — a year of your work is inside each of their arguments. so every ruling turns one side into people let down by somebody they counted as theirs. the version that would hold, in which both inheritances are being carried at their proper size, has never had a meeting it could be said in.
cost: nothing was lost in the handover. both halves of the place are still running, and the one a decisive successor would have thrown out is the half the trade now comes for. it took twenty-six years. under the portrait they will want a sentence about what your term was for, and none exists that both houses would sign.

lead: nobody has ever been introduced to half of you. the double goes into the room ahead of you, at a size that was never yours to set, and by the time you arrive it has already been called range.
sun: both of them are the work. the second is no relief from the first and the first is not what pays for the second — each is entered at full seriousness, each runs four years behind where a single-minded version of you would have it, and neither hedges the other. nobody in either field has met the half belonging to them without meeting the other one in the same sentence.
moon: six quiet months at one of them is not available to you. the spread is a dimension rather than a decision — there is no low setting on it — so the months get noticed, counted, and read as the other one having been dropped. what would make either half legible is a season with nobody looking, and nothing here folds away for a season.
pull: what you are known for is the doubling, at a size nothing in you can lower. it is also the single thing about you that no room has ever taken literally.
tension: versatile is the generous word and the ungenerous one is that you found an angle. both assume a decision was taken — that you sat down at some point and worked out that two would carry further than one. the actual arrangement, where neither could be put down without the other coming apart, is not something an audience has a category for, and from any seat in the room it looks precisely like the angle.
cost: two rooms admit you on sight, with no case made, where people who did one thing brilliantly are still arguing for entry at fifty. no piece of it has been judged on its own. arriving second is witnessed at the same scale as everything else, twice as often as anybody else manages it, before a room that settled years ago on which of the two was the excuse.

lead: The Turning finished one of the two completely, in a single season, with nothing of it left in your week. The Claws never ranked them and still does not, so what ended was a room and not a direction.
sun: each of the two had premises, people, a decade of work, and both were carried at their own full weight for twenty-two years, which is the only reason either of them was any good. the ending removed one set of doors. the load it was carrying is still in you, entire, at the weight it had when there was somewhere to set it down.
moon: what ended, ended in one piece, and what was owed survived it undiminished. the ones from the closed half still have every claim they had — the thing agreed in year two, the call on a bad night — and all of it is honoured by somebody with none of the machinery left to honour it with. nothing about the owing has moved a degree.
pull: you closed one of them absolutely and go on carrying what it was for. the room watching filed it as you finally choosing, and no choosing has occurred anywhere in it.
tension: everyone had the same theory of you for twenty years — that the second thing was the drag — and this was supposed to be the test of it. three years on, the half still running is going at exactly the rate it went at before, because the two directions were never the two jobs; they were inside each job the whole time. nobody has revised the theory. what gets said now is that you kept the wrong one.
cost: you can finish a thing outright, with no residue and no long decay for the people inside it to sit through. the direction does not finish. the ones you closed on have somebody who still holds their case entire and has nothing left to run it with, and their claims go on being paid in a currency the closure never touched.
